bridge: You know files, processes and units. Imagine your browser asking a fictional server for a page.
teaching:
### Follow the useful message

Your browser prepares an application message: a request for information. A protocol is a shared set of rules for the message's format, meaning and order. The programs at the ends of the exchange are endpoints.

Networks divide delivery into layers. The application layer gives the message its meaning. A transport protocol carries information between applications. IP handles addressing and forwarding across networks. A link carries data over the next local step.

### Keep the wrappers distinct

A header is extra information used to deliver or interpret data. A payload is the data that a particular wrapper carries. Adding one wrapper around another is encapsulation.

A router forwards packets toward another network. One forwarding step is a hop. A complete application message can span several packets; one packet is not automatically one complete request.

### Measure two different things

Latency is elapsed time between named events. Throughput is delivered data per unit time. A connection can take a long time to begin responding yet transfer a large file quickly once it starts.

In the example, the response returns after 80 ms. That is the supplied round-trip time, or RTT. One million bytes in two seconds is 500,000 bytes per second, or four million bits per second. Always state the unit.

### Know what your observation covers

A packet capture records traffic at a particular place and time. A packet missing from that capture may have passed elsewhere, been filtered out or arrived before recording began. Check the observation point before concluding it was lost.

### Separate capacity from delivered rate

Network bandwidth describes a potential transfer rate under stated conditions. Throughput is the rate actually delivered in your measurement. A nominal high-bandwidth connection can deliver less because of waiting, competing traffic, protocol overhead or another bottleneck. Both are rates; latency is a delay.
example:
Application: request "hello"
Transport: TCP carries a byte stream
Network: IP forwards packets toward destination
Link: local frame reaches next hop

Teaching timing:
send at 0 ms; response at 80 ms
payload delivered: 1,000,000 bytes in 2 seconds
RTT=80 ms; throughput=500,000 bytes/s=4,000,000 bits/s
explanation: The request leaves at 0 ms and its reply is observed at 80 ms, so round-trip time, or RTT, is 80 ms. This includes the chosen request/reply measurement path; it is not automatically the one-way link delay. Throughput uses a separate observation: \(1{,}000{,}000\) bytes over 2 seconds gives \(500{,}000\) bytes per second. Multiply by 8 bits per byte to get \(4{,}000{,}000\) bits per second. A rate describes how much data arrives per unit time; a delay describes how long an event takes. The wrapper for a local link may change at a router while the application’s request continues toward the same destination.
exercise: For response times 40,60,50 ms compute mean RTT. If 2,000 bytes arrive in 0.5 seconds, calculate bytes/s and bits/s. Draw which header belongs to link, IP, transport and application in a hypothetical request.
solution: Add the RTT measurements: \(40+60+50=150\) ms; divide by three to obtain mean RTT \(50\) ms. For throughput, \(2000/0.5=4000\) bytes/s, then \(4000\times8=32{,}000\) bits/s. A hypothetical packet drawing has an outer link header, then an IP header, then transport information, then application data. The exact headers depend on the selected protocols. These calculations count the stated payload bytes; they do not establish total wire traffic including headers or retransmissions.
challenge: A capture sees three packets of a five-packet transfer. Explain two reasons other than network loss that packets might be absent, and distinguish packet count from complete application messages.
challenge_solution: Capture start/end timing, capture filters and observation location can omit packets. Several packets may compose one message; retransmissions may repeat bytes. State the capture vantage point before inferring loss.
example_intro: Read the layer drawing and timing observations on paper. A header is control information added around data. A payload is the data carried by that layer. The two-second throughput observation is separate from the 80 ms request/reply observation.
